cls: Antispasmodic (combined musculotropic and anticholinergic smooth-muscle relaxant)
pharm: Relaxes visceral smooth muscle by a direct musculotropic (papaverine-like) action plus a mild anticholinergic (atropine-like) effect, relieving spasm and colicky pain.
quick: Typically 25-50 mg per dose (oral or parenteral) for spasm/colic
May be taken with or without food
Use only if clearly needed; has been used in labour - specialist judgement
Symptom relief, anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, palpitations, blurred vision)
summary: Camylofin (camylofin dihydrochloride) is an antispasmodic used to relieve smooth-muscle spasm and colicky pain in the gastrointestinal, biliary, and urinary tracts, in dysmenorrhoea, and, in some settings, to aid cervical dilatation in the active phase of labour. It works by a dual mechanism: a direct musculotropic relaxant action on smooth muscle (papaverine-like, via phosphodiesterase inhibition raising cyclic AMP) together with a mild anticholinergic (atropine-like) effect. Its anticholinergic activity is relatively weak, giving a reasonable safety profile, though dry mouth, palpitations, blurred vision, and pupillary dilatation can occur. It is frequently combined with analgesics such as paracetamol or diclofenac. Camylofin is not FDA-approved; it is marketed in India, parts of Europe, and other regions (data from drug monographs/SmPC-equivalent sources).
indications: Relief of smooth-muscle spasm and colicky pain - renal (ureteric) colic, biliary colic, gastrointestinal spasm
Adjunct for cervical dilatation in the active phase of labour (where locally approved)

dosage.d: Approximately 25-50 mg per dose, repeated as needed per product labeling
dosage.t: As needed for spasm (per local product)
dosage.n: Often combined with paracetamol or diclofenac

dosage.d: Approximately 25-50 mg by intramuscular or slow intravenous injection
dosage.n: For acute renal, biliary, or intestinal colic

dosage.d: Per local obstetric protocol to aid cervical dilatation

admin: May be given orally with or without food, or parenterally (IM/slow IV) for acute colic
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period needed to relieve spasm
Give slowly when administered intravenously and monitor for anticholinergic effects
Often used in fixed-dose combination with an analgesic (paracetamol or an NSAID)
Avoid in conditions where anticholinergic effects are hazardous (e.g., narrow-angle glaucoma, obstructive uropathy)
moa: Camylofin produces antispasmodic activity through a dual mechanism. Its predominant musculotropic action directly relaxes visceral smooth muscle in a papaverine-like manner, attributed to inhibition of phosphodiesterase with a resultant rise in intracellular cyclic AMP and reduced cytosolic calcium, relaxing the smooth muscle independent of the nerve supply. In addition, it has a mild neurotropic anticholinergic (atropine-like) effect, antagonising acetylcholine at muscarinic (predominantly M3) receptors on smooth muscle. The combined action relaxes smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal, biliary, and urinary tracts and the uterus, relieving spasm and colicky pain. Its anticholinergic potency is comparatively weak, so cardiac and secretory anticholinergic effects are usually modest.

absolute: Mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction or paralytic ileus
relative: Elderly patients (more sensitive to anticholinergic effects)
monitor: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, palpitations, blurred vision, urinary retention)
Heart rate and rhythm with parenteral use

preg: Data are limited. Camylofin should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed and the benefit justifies any risk; in some regions it has been used during the active phase of labour under specialist supervision.
lact: There are limited data on excretion into breast milk; use with caution during breastfeeding and only if the benefit outweighs the potential risk to the infant.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; specific dose-adjustment data are limited.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; specific dose-adjustment data are limited.

moderate: Other anticholinergic drugs (antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, antiparkinson agents) - additive anticholinergic effects
Other antispasmodics or smooth-muscle relaxants - additive effect
Prokinetics (e.g., metoclopramide) - opposing actions on gut motility
minor: CNS depressants - may add to dizziness/drowsiness
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol, which may add to drowsiness and dizziness.

monitoring: Anticholinergic adverse effects (dry mouth, palpitations, blurred vision, urinary retention)
Heart rate and rhythm, especially with parenteral dosing
Intraocular symptoms in patients at risk of glaucoma
counsel: This medicine relaxes the muscle cramps that cause your pain
You may notice a dry mouth, blurred vision, or a faster heartbeat - these usually pass
Do not drive or operate machinery if you feel dizzy or your vision is blurred
Tell your doctor if you have eye pressure problems (glaucoma), an enlarged prostate, or difficulty passing urine
Seek help for severe palpitations, confusion, or inability to pass urine
pk: Relief of spasm typically within minutes (parenteral) to ~30 minutes (oral)
Reached within about 1-2 hours after oral dosing
Several hours; redosed as needed for spasm
Store below 25-30 C; protect from light and moisture per product label
pearls: Dual mechanism: direct (papaverine-like) musculotropic relaxation plus mild (atropine-like) anticholinergic action
Anticholinergic potency is comparatively weak, giving a relatively favourable safety profile
Commonly used for renal, biliary, and intestinal colic and dysmenorrhoea, often combined with paracetamol or diclofenac
Avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma, obstructive uropathy, GI obstruction, and myasthenia gravis
Not FDA-approved - used in India, parts of Europe, and elsewhere; dosing per local product labeling
Watch for anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, palpitations, blurred vision, urinary retention), especially in the elderly
missed: If you are taking it on a regular schedule and miss a dose, take it when you remember; skip it if your next dose is near. As it is often used as needed for pain, only take it when you have spasm/colic. Do not double up.
overdose: Overdose produces an exaggerated anticholinergic syndrome: dry mouth and skin, flushing, mydriasis, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, agitation, and in severe cases hyperthermia, delirium, and arrhythmia. There is no specific antidote in routine use; management is supportive (cooling, hydration, cardiac monitoring), with physostigmine reserved for severe central anticholinergic toxicity under specialist supervision.
